# pdf-raster

Source: https://github.com/joshxfi/pdf-raster/blob/main/README.md

# pdf-raster

**Blazing fast, native PDF-to-image conversion for Node.js and Bun.**

`pdf-raster` renders PDF pages into high-quality image buffers using a
high-performance Rust engine. Built with `napi-rs` and `PDFium`, it is
optimized for server-side workflows like OCR pipelines, VLM (Vision Language
Model) inputs, and document previews.

[**Explore Documentation**](https://pdf-raster.omsimos.com/)

## ✨ Why pdf-raster?

- 🚀 **High Performance:** 4x–8x faster than `pdfjs-dist` canvas-based implementations in the included local benchmark run.
- 🦀 **Native Power:** Leverages Rust and PDFium for industry-standard rendering.
- 🛠️ **Simple API:** A single `convert()` function handles everything.
- 📦 **Memory Efficient:** Supports `Buffer` inputs for processing without temp files.
- 🎨 **Flexible Output:** Native support for `png`, `jpeg`, and `webp`.

## 📦 Install

```bash
# Using Bun
bun add pdf-raster

# Using PNPM
pnpm add pdf-raster

# Using NPM
npm install pdf-raster
```

## 📖 Quick Usage

```ts
import { convert } from "pdf-raster";
import { writeFile } from "node:fs/promises";

// Convert specific pages to high-quality WebP
const [page] = await convert("./report.pdf", {
  pages: [0], // 0-indexed page numbers
  dpi: 300, // Higher DPI is useful for OCR and VLM inputs
  outputFormat: "webp",
});

console.log(`Rendered page ${page.pageIndex} (${page.width}x${page.height})`);

// page.data is a Buffer of the encoded image
await writeFile("output.webp", page.data);
```

## 🛠 API Reference

### `convert(input, options?)`

#### `input`

- **Type:** `string | Buffer | Uint8Array | ArrayBuffer`
- **Description:** A file path to a PDF or an in-memory PDF byte source.

#### `options` (Optional)

| Option              | Type                        | Default | Description                                         |
| :------------------ | :-------------------------- | :------ | :-------------------------------------------------- |
| `pages`             | `number[]`                  | `all`   | Specific pages to render, using 0-indexed values.   |
| `dpi`               | `number`                    | `300`   | Resolution of the output image.                     |
| `outputFormat`      | `"png" \| "jpeg" \| "webp"` | `"png"` | Encoding format for the returned buffers.           |
| `password`          | `string`                    | `-`     | Password for encrypted PDFs.                        |
| `crop`              | `{ x, y, width, height }`   | `-`     | Crop rectangle in rendered image pixel coordinates. |
| `renderAnnotations` | `boolean`                   | `true`  | Whether to render annotations and form data.        |

#### Return Value: `Promise<ConvertedPage[]>`

```ts
type ConvertedPage = {
  pageIndex: number;
  data: Buffer;
  mimeType: "image/png" | "image/jpeg" | "image/webp";
  width: number;
  height: number;
  dpi: number;
};
```

## ⚡ Performance Benchmark

Tested on **Apple Silicon (M4)**. Results represent a local benchmark run
against the included fixture PDFs at `300 DPI`.

| Library                      | Avg/Page    | Relative Speed         |
| :--------------------------- | :---------- | :--------------------- |
| **pdf-raster**               | **0.86 ms** | **Baseline (Fastest)** |
| pdfjs-dist + @napi-rs/canvas | 5.98 ms     | ~6.9x slower           |
| pdfjs-dist + node-canvas     | 7.19 ms     | ~8.4x slower           |

> [!NOTE]
> Benchmark results are based on the included local fixtures. Performance will
> vary with PDF complexity and hardware. Run `bun run benchmark` on your own
> machine to compare against your environment.

## 🌍 Runtime & Platform Support

This package uses native bindings and is intended for **server-side environments only**.

| Runtime           | Supported |
| :---------------- | :-------- |
| **Node.js**       | ✅ Yes    |
| **Bun**           | ✅ Yes    |
| **Browser**       | ❌ No     |
| **Edge Runtimes** | ❌ No     |

**Supported Architectures:**

- **OS:** Linux (gnu), macOS, Windows
- **Arch:** x64, arm64

> [!CAUTION]
> Do not import this into browser bundles, React Client Components, or Vercel Edge Functions.

## 🛠 Local Development

This repository is a Bun + Turborepo monorepo.

1. **Setup:** `bun install`
2. **Native Binaries:** `bun run pdfium:download`
3. **Build:** `bun run build`
4. **Test:** `bun run test`
5. **Benchmark:** `bun run benchmark`

### Workspace layout

- `core/` - the published `pdf-raster` package
- `example/` - the polished internal demo app using the local workspace package
- `consumer/` - a minimal Next.js app for validating the published npm package
- `docs/` - the hosted documentation source
- `benchmark/` - internal performance comparisons against `pdfjs-dist`

MIT

# api-reference.mdx

Source: https://github.com/joshxfi/pdf-raster/blob/main/docs/content/docs/api-reference.mdx

title: API reference
description: Inputs, options, outputs, and stable error codes for convert().

## `convert(input, options?)`

```ts
function convert(
  input: string | Buffer | Uint8Array | ArrayBuffer,
  options?: ConvertOptions,
): Promise<ConvertedPage[]>;
```

## Inputs

<TypeTable
  type={{
    "file path": {
      type: "string",
      description: "Absolute or relative path to a PDF on disk.",
    },
    Buffer: {
      type: "Buffer",
      description: "PDF bytes already loaded into memory.",
    },
    Uint8Array: {
      type: "Uint8Array",
      description: "Typed-array PDF bytes.",
    },
    ArrayBuffer: {
      type: "ArrayBuffer",
      description: "Browser-style binary buffer passed from server code.",
    },
  }}
/>

## `ConvertOptions`

<TypeTable
  type={{
    pages: {
      type: "number[]",
      description: "Zero-based page indices to render.",
      required: false,
      default: "all pages",
    },
    dpi: {
      type: "number",
      description: "Target raster DPI.",
      required: false,
      default: "300",
    },
    outputFormat: {
      type: '"png" | "jpeg" | "webp"',
      description: "Output format. PNG is the default.",
      required: false,
      default: '"png"',
    },
    password: {
      type: "string",
      description: "Password for encrypted PDFs.",
      required: false,
    },
    crop: {
      type: "{ x; y; width; height }",
      description: "Crop rectangle applied after rendering.",
      required: false,
      typeDescription:
        "{ x: number; y: number; width: number; height: number }",
    },
    renderAnnotations: {
      type: "boolean",
      description: "Whether annotations and form data should be rendered.",
      required: false,
      default: "true",
    },
  }}
/>

<Callout type="warning" title="Page indices are zero-based">
  `pages: [0]` means the first page. `pages: [1]` means the second page.

## `ConvertedPage`

<TypeTable
  type={{
    pageIndex: {
      type: "number",
      description: "Zero-based page index in the source document.",
      required: true,
    },
    data: {
      type: "Buffer",
      description: "Encoded image bytes for the rendered page.",
      required: true,
    },
    mimeType: {
      type: '"image/png" | "image/jpeg" | "image/webp"',
      description: "MIME type of the returned image buffer.",
      required: true,
    },
    width: {
      type: "number",
      description: "Rendered image width in pixels.",
      required: true,
    },
    height: {
      type: "number",
      description: "Rendered image height in pixels.",
      required: true,
    },
    dpi: {
      type: "number",
      description: "Effective DPI used to render the page.",
      required: true,
    },
  }}
/>

## Error codes

<TypeTable
  type={{
    INVALID_INPUT: {
      type: "PdfToImagesError",
      description: "The input was not a supported file path or binary type.",
    },
    INVALID_OPTIONS: {
      type: "PdfToImagesError",
      description:
        "One or more options were invalid, such as a non-positive DPI or unsupported output format.",
    },
    INVALID_PAGE_INDEX: {
      type: "PdfToImagesError",
      description: "A requested page index was negative or out of range.",
    },
    INVALID_CROP: {
      type: "PdfToImagesError",
      description:
        "The crop rectangle was malformed or exceeded the rendered page bounds.",
    },
    PASSWORD_ERROR: {
      type: "PdfToImagesError",
      description: "The PDF password was missing or incorrect.",
    },
    MALFORMED_PDF: {
      type: "PdfToImagesError",
      description: "The PDF could not be parsed by PDFium.",
    },
    PDFIUM_UNAVAILABLE: {
      type: "PdfToImagesError",
      description:
        "The native PDFium library or binding could not be initialized.",
    },
    RENDER_ERROR: {
      type: "PdfToImagesError",
      description:
        "An unexpected native rendering failure occurred after input validation.",
    },
  }}
/>

# benchmark.mdx

Source: https://github.com/joshxfi/pdf-raster/blob/main/docs/content/docs/benchmark.mdx

title: Benchmark
description: Understand the current local benchmark setup and sample results for pdf-raster.

<Callout type="info" title="Sample local results">
  The numbers on this page are from a local benchmark run against the included
  fixture PDFs. Treat them as sample measurements, not universal guarantees.

## What the benchmark compares

The benchmark currently compares three implementations on the same input PDFs
and settings:

- `pdf-raster`
- `pdfjs-dist + @napi-rs/canvas`
- `pdfjs-dist + node-canvas`

## Run it

```bash
bun run benchmark
```

## Default settings

<Steps>
  <Step>
    Use the valid fixture PDFs under `core/test/fixtures`.
  </Step>
  <Step>
    Render at `dpi=300` with `output=png`.
  </Step>
  <Step>
    Execute one warmup run, then repeated measured runs for each backend.
  </Step>
</Steps>

<Callout type="warning" title="node-canvas requirement">
  The benchmark workspace includes both `@napi-rs/canvas` and `node-canvas`.
  Depending on your machine, `node-canvas` may require native system
  prerequisites before the benchmark can run successfully.

## Sample output

```text
File: multi-page.pdf
Settings: dpi=300, output=png, pages=all, warmups=1, runs=5
Input size: 842 B
Library                       Pages  Avg total  P50 total  Avg/page  Avg bytes
----------------------------  -----  ---------  ---------  --------  ---------
pdf-raster                    2      1.72 ms    1.70 ms    0.86 ms   36.2 KB
pdfjs-dist + @napi-rs/canvas  2      11.96 ms   11.91 ms   5.98 ms   22.6 KB
pdfjs-dist + node-canvas      2      14.37 ms   14.37 ms   7.19 ms   22.8 KB

Relative speed (pdf-raster vs pdfjs-dist + @napi-rs/canvas): total 6.94x
Relative speed (pdf-raster vs pdfjs-dist + node-canvas): total 8.35x

File: single-page.pdf
Settings: dpi=300, output=png, pages=all, warmups=1, runs=5
Input size: 583 B
Library                       Pages  Avg total  P50 total  Avg/page  Avg bytes
----------------------------  -----  ---------  ---------  --------  ---------
pdf-raster                    1      1.29 ms    1.00 ms    1.29 ms   13.4 KB
pdfjs-dist + @napi-rs/canvas  1      5.81 ms    5.83 ms    5.81 ms   7.6 KB
pdfjs-dist + node-canvas      1      7.25 ms    7.26 ms    7.25 ms   7.8 KB

Relative speed (pdf-raster vs pdfjs-dist + @napi-rs/canvas): total 4.51x
Relative speed (pdf-raster vs pdfjs-dist + node-canvas): total 5.63x
```

## How to read the multipliers

The relative speed line is a multiplier, not a percentage.

- If the benchmark says `6.94x`, it means the comparison backend took `6.94`
  times as long on that metric.
- In other words, `pdf-raster` was `6.94x` faster on that sample.

## What this benchmark is useful for

- compare end-to-end conversion speed on the included fixtures
- spot regressions between local runs
- compare the current PDFium-based package against `pdfjs-dist` canvas
  backends

Use it as a practical engineering comparison tool, not as a universal claim
about every PDF or every deployment environment.

# errors-and-troubleshooting.mdx

Source: https://github.com/joshxfi/pdf-raster/blob/main/docs/content/docs/errors-and-troubleshooting.mdx

title: Errors and troubleshooting
description: Understand stable error codes and the most common failure scenarios.

## Stable error model

The package throws `PdfToImagesError` with a stable `code`.

That lets you distinguish:

- bad caller input
- malformed or encrypted documents
- native runtime setup failures
- rendering failures

## Common problems

<Accordions type="single">
  <Accordion title="I got INVALID_PAGE_INDEX">
    A requested page index does not exist in the document, or the value was not
    a non-negative integer. Remember that page indices are zero-based.
  </Accordion>
  <Accordion title="I got INVALID_OPTIONS">
    Check `dpi`, `pages`, and `outputFormat`. Supported output formats are
    `png`, `jpeg`, and `webp`.
  </Accordion>
  <Accordion title="I got MALFORMED_PDF">
    PDFium could not parse the file. This usually means the uploaded bytes are
    not a valid PDF or the file is structurally corrupted.
  </Accordion>
  <Accordion title="I got PASSWORD_ERROR">
    The document is encrypted and the password was missing or incorrect.
  </Accordion>
  <Accordion title="I got PDFIUM_UNAVAILABLE">
    The native PDFium library could not be loaded. In this monorepo, run
    `bun run pdfium:download` and rebuild the package.
  </Accordion>
  <Accordion title="I got RENDER_ERROR">
    Input validation succeeded, but the native render failed. Start by testing
    the same document with the package test flow and checking the local PDFium
    setup.
  </Accordion>
</Accordions>

## Production guidance

If you expose conversion through an API:

- map stable error codes into HTTP status codes
- log the native failure message on the server
- avoid returning full native diagnostics to untrusted clients

# example-patterns.mdx

Source: https://github.com/joshxfi/pdf-raster/blob/main/docs/content/docs/example-patterns.mdx

title: Examples and patterns
description: Choose the right integration pattern for Node.js, Next.js, and downstream image workflows.

Use this page as an index to the most common ways teams integrate the library.

<Cards>
  <Card title="Node.js recipes" href="/docs/examples-node">
    File-path conversion, in-memory buffers, and selected-page usage.
  </Card>
  <Card title="Next.js route handlers" href="/docs/examples-nextjs">
    The smallest correct server-side pattern for App Router APIs.
  </Card>
  <Card title="Next.js upload + preview" href="/docs/examples-nextjs-full-flow">
    Add a client upload form, call a route handler, and render every page image.
  </Card>
  <Card title="Downstream integrations" href="/docs/examples-ocr-vlm">
    Pass rendered page images into OCR, AI SDK image prompts, or other consumers.
  </Card>
</Cards>

## Which pattern should you choose?

<Accordions type="single">
  <Accordion title="I already have a PDF on disk">
    Start with the Node.js file-path example. It is the simplest call shape and
    works well for backend jobs or batch pipelines.
  </Accordion>
  <Accordion title="My PDF arrives over HTTP or from object storage">
    Use the in-memory buffer pattern so you can keep everything off disk.
  </Accordion>
  <Accordion title="I need to expose this behind a web UI">
    Start with the route-handler example if you only need the server API. Use
    the full Next.js upload-and-preview example if you also need a client page
    that renders every returned image.
  </Accordion>
  <Accordion title="I need smaller preview payloads">
    Keep PNG as the default when quality matters most. Use WebP or JPEG when
    you want to shrink response sizes for previews or downstream transport.
  </Accordion>
  <Accordion title="I want to send pages into another system">
    Convert first, then pass the rendered page images into whatever comes next,
    whether that is OCR, an image API, a multimodal model, or your own
    processing pipeline.
  </Accordion>
</Accordions>

# examples-nextjs-full-flow.mdx

Source: https://github.com/joshxfi/pdf-raster/blob/main/docs/content/docs/examples-nextjs-full-flow.mdx

title: Next.js upload and preview example
description: Build a simple App Router flow with a client upload form, a Node.js route handler, and image previews for every returned page.

<Callout type="warning" title="Keep the native package on the server">
  Import `pdf-raster` only inside the route handler. The client page
  should only send `FormData` and render the returned image payloads.

This example shows a complete App Router flow:

<Steps>
  <Step>
    The client page uploads a PDF with `FormData`.
  </Step>
  <Step>
    The route handler validates the upload, converts the PDF, and returns one
    response object per page.
  </Step>
  <Step>
    The client renders every returned image with `next/image`.
  </Step>
</Steps>

## File structure

<Files>
  <Folder name="app" defaultOpen>
    <File name="page.tsx" />
    <Folder name="api" defaultOpen>
      <Folder name="convert" defaultOpen>
        <File name="route.ts" />
      </Folder>
    </Folder>
  </Folder>
</Files>

## Route handler

```ts
import { NextResponse } from "next/server";
import { convert, PdfToImagesError } from "pdf-raster";

export const runtime = "nodejs";

function errorResponse(code: string, message: string, status: number) {
  return NextResponse.json({ code, message }, { status });
}

export async function POST(request: Request) {
  try {
    const formData = await request.formData();
    const upload = formData.get("file");

    if (!(upload instanceof File)) {
      return errorResponse("INVALID_INPUT", "Missing PDF upload.", 400);
    }

    const lowerName = upload.name.toLowerCase();
    const isPdf =
      upload.type === "application/pdf" || lowerName.endsWith(".pdf");

    if (!isPdf) {
      return errorResponse("INVALID_INPUT", "Only PDF uploads are supported.", 400);
    }

    const buffer = Buffer.from(await upload.arrayBuffer());
    const pages = await convert(buffer, {
      dpi: 300,
      outputFormat: "png",
    });

    return NextResponse.json({
      pages: pages.map((page) => ({
        pageIndex: page.pageIndex,
        width: page.width,
        height: page.height,
        dpi: page.dpi,
        mimeType: page.mimeType,
        src: `data:${page.mimeType};base64,${page.data.toString("base64")}`,
      })),
    });
  } catch (error) {
    if (error instanceof PdfToImagesError) {
      return errorResponse(error.code, error.message, 400);
    }

    return errorResponse(
      "RENDER_ERROR",
      "Unexpected conversion failure.",
      500,
    );
  }
}
```

## Client page

```tsx
"use client";

import Image from "next/image";
import { useState } from "react";

type ConvertedPage = {
  pageIndex: number;
  width: number;
  height: number;
  dpi: number;
  mimeType: string;
  src: string;
};

export default function Page() {
  const [file, setFile] = useState<File | null>(null);
  const [pages, setPages] = useState<ConvertedPage[]>([]);
  const [error, setError] = useState<string | null>(null);
  const [isLoading, setIsLoading] = useState(false);

  async function handleSubmit(event: React.FormEvent<HTMLFormElement>) {
    event.preventDefault();

    if (!file) {
      setError("Choose a PDF before converting.");
      return;
    }

    setError(null);
    setIsLoading(true);
    setPages([]);

    const formData = new FormData();
    formData.set("file", file);

    const response = await fetch("/api/convert", {
      method: "POST",
      body: formData,
    });

    const payload = await response.json();

    if (!response.ok) {
      setError(payload.message ?? "Conversion failed.");
      setIsLoading(false);
      return;
    }

    setPages(payload.pages ?? []);
    setIsLoading(false);
  }

  return (
    <main>
      <form onSubmit={handleSubmit}>
        <input
          type="file"
          accept="application/pdf,.pdf"
          onChange={(event) => setFile(event.currentTarget.files?.[0] ?? null)}
        />
        <button type="submit" disabled={isLoading}>
          {isLoading ? "Converting..." : "Convert PDF"}
        </button>
      </form>

      {error ? <p>{error}</p> : null}

      <section>
        {pages.map((page) => (
          <article key={page.pageIndex}>
            <h2>Page {page.pageIndex + 1}</h2>
            <p>
              {page.width} × {page.height} at {page.dpi} DPI
            </p>
            <Image
              src={page.src}
              alt={`Rendered PDF page ${page.pageIndex + 1}`}
              width={page.width}
              height={page.height}
              unoptimized
            />
          </article>
        ))}
      </section>
    </main>
  );
}
```

## Why this pattern works

- the browser never imports the native package
- the route stays small and can normalize errors for the UI
- the client gets everything it needs to render all page previews immediately

<Callout type="info" title="Good for docs, demos, and small previews">
  Returning `data:` URLs keeps the example easy to understand. For larger jobs,
  prefer storing the rendered images server-side and returning references
  instead of base64-encoding every page into JSON.

If you only need the API endpoint and not the upload UI, use the
[smaller route-handler example](/docs/examples-nextjs) instead.

---

# examples-nextjs.mdx

Source: https://github.com/joshxfi/pdf-raster/blob/main/docs/content/docs/examples-nextjs.mdx

title: Next.js route handler example
description: The smallest correct Next.js server-side pattern for converting PDFs inside App Router.

<Callout type="warning" title="Node runtime only">
  Keep this package in a Node.js route handler or other server-only code. Do
  not import it into the client or Edge runtime.

This page shows only the server route. If you also want a client upload form
and a preview grid that renders every returned page image, use the
[full Next.js upload and preview example](/docs/examples-nextjs-full-flow).

## Example route handler

<Files>
  <Folder name="app" defaultOpen>
    <Folder name="api" defaultOpen>
      <Folder name="convert" defaultOpen>
        <File name="route.ts" />
      </Folder>
    </Folder>
  </Folder>
</Files>

```ts
import { NextResponse } from "next/server";
import { convert, PdfToImagesError } from "pdf-raster";

export const runtime = "nodejs";

export async function POST(request: Request) {
  try {
    const formData = await request.formData();
    const upload = formData.get("file");
    const isPdf =
      upload instanceof File &&
      (upload.type === "application/pdf" ||
        upload.name.toLowerCase().endsWith(".pdf"));

    if (!isPdf || !(upload instanceof File)) {
      return NextResponse.json(
        { code: "INVALID_INPUT", message: "Missing PDF upload." },
        { status: 400 },
      );
    }

    const bytes = Buffer.from(await upload.arrayBuffer());
    const pages = await convert(bytes, {
      pages: [0],
      outputFormat: "webp",
      dpi: 300,
    });

    return NextResponse.json({
      pages: pages.map((page) => ({
        pageIndex: page.pageIndex,
        width: page.width,
        height: page.height,
        dpi: page.dpi,
        mimeType: page.mimeType,
        src: `data:${page.mimeType};base64,${page.data.toString("base64")}`,
      })),
    });
  } catch (error) {
    if (error instanceof PdfToImagesError) {
      return NextResponse.json(
        { code: error.code, message: error.message },
        { status: 400 },
      );
    }

    return NextResponse.json(
      { code: "RENDER_ERROR", message: "Unexpected conversion failure." },
      { status: 500 },
    );
  }
}
```

This route shape is useful when:

- your frontend is already built and only needs an API endpoint
- you want to keep the native package isolated to one server route
- you plan to return small preview payloads, object-storage URLs, or other
  app-specific response shapes

## Why a route handler works well

- keeps the native binding on the server
- accepts uploads directly
- can normalize errors into stable API responses
- lets the client render previews without touching PDFium directly

<Callout type="info" title="Use data URLs for small previews">
  Returning `data:` URLs is convenient for demos and document previews. For
  larger jobs, it is usually better to return file handles, object-storage URLs,
  or another server-side reference instead of base64-encoding every page into
  JSON.

If you want to see the matching client page that uploads a PDF and renders the
returned images, continue to the
[full Next.js upload and preview example](/docs/examples-nextjs-full-flow).

---

# examples-node.mdx

Source: https://github.com/joshxfi/pdf-raster/blob/main/docs/content/docs/examples-node.mdx

title: Node.js examples
description: Common Node and Bun usage patterns for convert().

Use these patterns when conversion happens entirely in server code or a worker.

## Convert a PDF from disk

```ts
import { writeFile } from "node:fs/promises";
import { convert } from "pdf-raster";

const [firstPage] = await convert("./report.pdf", {
  pages: [0],
  dpi: 300,
});

await writeFile("./report-page-1.png", firstPage.data);

console.log(firstPage.mimeType);
// "image/png"
```

This is the simplest shape when the PDF already lives on disk and you want to
save or inspect the rendered image output directly.

## Convert selected pages from a larger document

```ts
import { convert } from "pdf-raster";

const pages = await convert("./report.pdf", {
  pages: [0, 3, 4],
  dpi: 300,
});
```

## Request a different output format

```ts
import { convert } from "pdf-raster";

const pages = await convert("./report.pdf", {
  outputFormat: "webp",
  dpi: 200,
});

console.log(pages[0].mimeType);
// "image/webp"
```

Use PNG when you want the safest default. Use WebP or JPEG when smaller payloads
matter more than lossless output.

## Convert from an in-memory buffer

```ts
import { readFile } from "node:fs/promises";
import { convert } from "pdf-raster";

const bytes = await readFile("./invoice.pdf");
const pages = await convert(bytes, {
  dpi: 300,
});
```

## Path vs buffer

<CodeBlockTabs defaultValue="path">
  <CodeBlockTabsList>
    <CodeBlockTabsTrigger value="path">Path input</CodeBlockTabsTrigger>
    <CodeBlockTabsTrigger value="buffer">Buffer input</CodeBlockTabsTrigger>
  </CodeBlockTabsList>
  <CodeBlockTab value="path">

```ts
await convert("./document.pdf");
```

  </CodeBlockTab>
  <CodeBlockTab value="buffer">

```ts
await convert(pdfBuffer);
```

  </CodeBlockTab>
</CodeBlockTabs>

Use a path when the file already lives on disk. Use a buffer when the PDF came
from an upload, queue payload, or external storage SDK.

---

# examples-ocr-vlm.mdx

Source: https://github.com/joshxfi/pdf-raster/blob/main/docs/content/docs/examples-ocr-vlm.mdx

title: OCR and VLM examples
description: Pass converted page images into OCR engines or multimodal SDKs.

These examples show how to pass converted page images into OCR and multimodal
tools after rendering.

<Callout type="info" title="Choose a format for the downstream tool">
  PNG is the safest default. Use WebP or JPEG if you want smaller payloads and
  the downstream tool accepts those formats.

## Tesseract.js

```ts
import { convert } from "pdf-raster";
import { createWorker } from "tesseract.js";

const worker = await createWorker("eng");
const [page] = await convert("./scan.pdf", {
  pages: [0],
  dpi: 300,
});

const result = await worker.recognize(page.data);
console.log(result.data.text);
```

`page.data` is already an encoded image buffer, so it can be passed directly
into OCR libraries that accept image bytes.

## AI SDK `generateText`

```ts
import { convert } from "pdf-raster";
import { generateText } from "ai";
import { openai } from "@ai-sdk/openai";

const [page] = await convert("./invoice.pdf", {
  pages: [0],
  dpi: 300,
});

const { text } = await generateText({
  model: openai("gpt-4.1"),
  messages: [
    {
      role: "user",
      content: [
        { type: "text", text: "Extract all visible text from this page." },
        { type: "image", image: page.data },
      ],
    },
  ],
});
```

The same pattern works for other image-capable SDKs: convert first, then pass
`page.data` and `page.mimeType` into the next system.

## Why the handoff is simple

The converted page result is already shaped for downstream use:

- `page.data` is the image payload
- `page.mimeType` tells the consumer what it is
- `page.width`, `page.height`, and `page.dpi` help with validation and metrics

## Boundary to preserve

<Callout type="info" title="Keep responsibilities separated">
  `pdf-raster` handles the PDF-to-image step. OCR engines, VLM
  providers, and post-processing can be layered on top in app code or separate
  packages.

---

# index.mdx

Source: https://github.com/joshxfi/pdf-raster/blob/main/docs/content/docs/index.mdx

title: Introduction
description: What pdf-raster is for, what it returns, and where it fits in backend and document-processing workflows.

<Callout type="info" title="Single responsibility">
  `pdf-raster` converts PDF pages into image buffers with a single
  native API.

`pdf-raster` is a native server-side library for turning PDFs into
page images quickly.

It fits cleanly anywhere you need page images instead of PDF bytes:

<Steps>
  <Step>
    Start with a PDF from disk, object storage, an upload, or another API.
  </Step>
  <Step>
    Use `pdf-raster` to render the document into page images.
  </Step>
  <Step>
    Use the output in previews, background jobs, OCR flows, VLM prompts, or
    any other downstream image workflow.
  </Step>
</Steps>

## What the library does

<Cards>
  <Card title="One public API" href="/docs/api-reference">
    The package centers on `convert(input, options?)`.
  </Card>
  <Card title="Native rendering" href="/docs/runtime-and-environment">
    Rendering is handled through Rust, `napi-rs`, and PDFium.
  </Card>
  <Card title="Lossless output" href="/docs/quickstart">
    Each page comes back as an image `Buffer` with dimensions and DPI metadata.
  </Card>
</Cards>

## What it intentionally does not do

- no browser runtime support
- no document editing, annotation, or extraction APIs

That narrow API keeps the package easy to reason about. You can use the output
for previews, storage, background jobs, OCR, VLM prompts, or other downstream
processing without changing how the conversion layer works.

## Output shape

Each page is returned as:

```ts
type ConvertedPage = {
  pageIndex: number;
  data: Buffer;
  mimeType: "image/png" | "image/jpeg" | "image/webp";
  width: number;
  height: number;
  dpi: number;
};
```

## Why this package exists

Many systems do not want PDF bytes directly. They want page images that are:

- lossless
- easy to inspect
- high enough resolution for reading and analysis
- straightforward to pass into downstream APIs

This package makes that conversion step small, explicit, and fast.

## Read next

<Cards>
  <Card title="Installation" href="/docs/installation">
    Install the package and understand the native runtime model.
  </Card>
  <Card title="Quickstart" href="/docs/quickstart">
    Convert a PDF into page images with the real API.
  </Card>
  <Card title="Examples" href="/docs/example-patterns">
    Choose the right recipe for Node, Next.js, and downstream image workflows.
  </Card>
</Cards>

# installation.mdx

Source: https://github.com/joshxfi/pdf-raster/blob/main/docs/content/docs/installation.mdx

title: Installation
description: Install the package and understand what gets pulled in at runtime.

## Install the package

<CodeBlockTabs defaultValue="bun">
  <CodeBlockTabsList>
    <CodeBlockTabsTrigger value="bun">bun</CodeBlockTabsTrigger>
    <CodeBlockTabsTrigger value="pnpm">pnpm</CodeBlockTabsTrigger>
    <CodeBlockTabsTrigger value="npm">npm</CodeBlockTabsTrigger>
  </CodeBlockTabsList>
  <CodeBlockTab value="bun">

```bash
bun add pdf-raster
```

  </CodeBlockTab>
  <CodeBlockTab value="pnpm">

```bash
pnpm add pdf-raster
```

  </CodeBlockTab>
  <CodeBlockTab value="npm">

```bash
npm install pdf-raster
```

  </CodeBlockTab>
</CodeBlockTabs>

## Runtime model

<Callout type="warning" title="Server-side only">
  This package is meant for Node.js and Bun. Do not import it into browser
  bundles.

The library is native and server-side:

- supported runtimes: Node.js and Bun
- rendering backend: PDFium
- primary output: image `Buffer`s for each page

Use it in:

- backend jobs
- API routes and route handlers
- worker processes
- document-processing services

## What the package contains

Installing `pdf-raster` gives you:

- the JavaScript API
- a native `.node` binding for the current platform
- the matching PDFium shared library used for rendering

The goal is still a thin JavaScript surface with native rendering under the
hood.

# local-development.mdx

Source: https://github.com/joshxfi/pdf-raster/blob/main/docs/content/docs/local-development.mdx

title: Local development
description: Prepare PDFium, build the native package, and validate the local development setup in this monorepo.

Use this page if you are working on `pdf-raster` itself inside the
monorepo. If you only want to install and use the package, start with
[Installation](/docs/installation).

## Local development flow

<Steps>
  <Step>
    Download or refresh the local PDFium cache:

```bash
bun run pdfium:download
```

  </Step>
  <Step>
    Build the native package:

```bash
bun run --filter pdf-raster build
```

  </Step>
  <Step>
    Run the package tests to validate the local native path:

```bash
bun run --filter pdf-raster test
```

  </Step>
</Steps>

## Environment notes

<TypeTable
  type={{
    PDFIUM_LIB_PATH: {
      type: "string",
      description:
        "Optional explicit path to a local PDFium shared library.",
      required: false,
    },
    PDFIUM_CACHE_DIR: {
      type: "string",
      description:
        "Optional override for the repo-local PDFium cache directory.",
      required: false,
    },
    PDFIUM_RELEASE: {
      type: "string",
      description:
        "Optional release selector for the cached or downloaded PDFium binary.",
      required: false,
      default: '"latest"',
    },
  }}
/>

## Typical commands

<Files>
  <File name="bun run pdfium:download" />
  <File name="bun run --filter pdf-raster build" />
  <File name="bun run --filter pdf-raster test" />
</Files>

## If the native setup breaks

<Steps>
  <Step>
    Make sure the package is built for the current platform.
  </Step>
  <Step>
    Refresh the local PDFium cache with `bun run pdfium:download`.
  </Step>
  <Step>
    Rebuild the package with `bun run --filter pdf-raster build`.
  </Step>
  <Step>
    Run `bun run --filter pdf-raster test` to validate the native
    path.
  </Step>
</Steps>

# quickstart.mdx

Source: https://github.com/joshxfi/pdf-raster/blob/main/docs/content/docs/quickstart.mdx

title: Quickstart
description: Convert PDFs into page images from a file path or an in-memory buffer.

`convert()` is the only public entrypoint you need to learn first.

## Convert all pages from a file path

```ts
import { convert } from "pdf-raster";

const pages = await convert("./report.pdf");

for (const page of pages) {
  console.log({
    pageIndex: page.pageIndex,
    outputFormat: page.mimeType,
    width: page.width,
    height: page.height,
    dpi: page.dpi,
  });
}
```

<Callout type="info" title="Default behavior">
  If `pages` is omitted, the full document is rendered. If `outputFormat` is
  omitted, the output defaults to PNG.

## What one page looks like

Each item in `pages` is a complete rendered image result:

```ts
const [page] = await convert("./report.pdf");

console.log({
  pageIndex: page.pageIndex,
  mimeType: page.mimeType,
  width: page.width,
  height: page.height,
  dpi: page.dpi,
  bytes: page.data.byteLength,
});

// {
//   pageIndex: 0,
//   mimeType: "image/png",
//   width: 833,
//   height: 417,
//   dpi: 300,
//   bytes: 14032
// }
```

The actual image bytes are in `page.data`, so you can write them to disk,
return them from an API, or pass them into another service directly.

## Convert selected pages

Page indices are zero-based:

```ts
import { convert } from "pdf-raster";

const pages = await convert("./report.pdf", {
  pages: [0, 2],
  dpi: 300,
});
```

## Choose an output format

PNG is the default, but you can request another encoded format when needed:

```ts
import { convert } from "pdf-raster";

const pages = await convert("./report.pdf", {
  outputFormat: "webp",
});

console.log(pages[0].mimeType);
// "image/webp"
```

## Convert from an in-memory buffer

<CodeBlockTabs defaultValue="path">
  <CodeBlockTabsList>
    <CodeBlockTabsTrigger value="path">File path</CodeBlockTabsTrigger>
    <CodeBlockTabsTrigger value="buffer">In-memory buffer</CodeBlockTabsTrigger>
  </CodeBlockTabsList>
  <CodeBlockTab value="path">

```ts
import { convert } from "pdf-raster";

const pages = await convert("./invoice.pdf", {
  dpi: 300,
});
```

  </CodeBlockTab>
  <CodeBlockTab value="buffer">

```ts
import { readFile } from "node:fs/promises";
import { convert } from "pdf-raster";

const bytes = await readFile("./invoice.pdf");
const pages = await convert(bytes, {
  dpi: 300,
});
```

  </CodeBlockTab>
</CodeBlockTabs>

## Understand the result

Every page includes:

- `pageIndex`
- `data` as an encoded image `Buffer`
- `mimeType`
- `width`
- `height`
- `dpi`

These values are enough to:

- save the image
- display it in a UI
- upload it to another API
- feed it into downstream processing

## Common first mistakes

<Accordions type="single">
  <Accordion title="Why are page numbers zero-based?">
    The API uses JavaScript-style zero-based indices because `pages` is an
    array of page indices, not human-readable page labels.
  </Accordion>
  <Accordion title="Why does the library return image buffers instead of file paths?">
    Returning bytes keeps the package flexible for APIs, workers, storage, and
    other downstream consumers without forcing filesystem writes.
  </Accordion>
  <Accordion title="Should I call this in a browser component?">
    No. Keep it in server code only.
  </Accordion>
</Accordions>

## Read next

- [API reference](/docs/api-reference)
- [Examples and patterns](/docs/example-patterns)

# runtime-and-environment.mdx

Source: https://github.com/joshxfi/pdf-raster/blob/main/docs/content/docs/runtime-and-environment.mdx

title: Runtime and environment
description: Understand supported runtimes and the native PDFium dependency model.

## Supported runtimes

`pdf-raster` is designed for:

- Node.js
- Bun

It is not designed for:

- browsers
- React client components
- Edge runtime
- WebAssembly

## Why server-side only

The package loads a native binding and a platform-specific PDFium library. That
is the right tradeoff for throughput and installation simplicity on the server,
but it means the package should stay on the backend side of your app.

<Callout type="warning" title="Next.js runtime choice">
  In Next.js, keep `pdf-raster` inside Node.js route handlers or
  other server-only code. Do not run it in Edge routes.

## Native dependency model

At runtime, the package needs:

- the `napi-rs` native binding
- a matching PDFium library for the current platform

In this monorepo, PDFium is cached locally and bundled during package builds.

## If the library fails to initialize

See [Errors and troubleshooting](/docs/errors-and-troubleshooting). If you are
working on the package locally, also see [Local development](/docs/local-development).

---

# docs

Source: https://github.com/joshxfi/pdf-raster/blob/main/docs/README.md

# docs

This app is the documentation site for `pdf-raster`, built with
Fumadocs and Next.js.

## Commands

```bash
bun run dev
bun run check-types
bun run build
```

The docs app runs on port `3001` in local development.

## Content layout

- `app/(home)`: landing page
- `app/docs`: documentation routes
- `content/docs`: MDX content for the library
- `lib/source.ts`: Fumadocs content source loader
- `lib/layout.shared.tsx`: shared docs metadata and repo links

## Notes

- the app stays standalone on Fumadocs UI
- `check-types` runs Fumadocs MDX generation, Next type generation, and `tsc`
- docs content is currently focused on `pdf-raster`
